title: The Heir of Karavira
story:
The gates of Karavira opened before the column had even reached them, and the king came out to meet it as a storm comes out of a clear sky.

King Shrigala drove out on a chariot that shone like the car of Indra, quick-coursing horses and golden axles, quivers inexhaustible, and at the sight of him the earth itself was said to sink a little under his wheels. He had heard how the armies of the kings had fared on Mount Gomanta, and the report had not frightened him. It had offended him. In the middle of the open field, with his army ranked behind him, he reined in before Krishna and called out so that all could hear.

"I have heard of your work against the stupid kings at Gomanta, who had no leader," he said. "I am the emperor of the world. You are alone, and I am with my army, so I should not fight you with all these men. Come, I will fight you alone, and one of us will meet his death in a fair fight. If you are slain, I shall be the only Vasudeva in the world. And if I am slain, you shall be the only one."

Krishna heard him out without changing expression. "Strike me as you wish," he said.

Shrigala's answer was a net of arrows. He showered Krishna with shafts and maces and weapons covered with flame, and Krishna stood where he was, motionless, like a mountain taking rain. Only when the assault had spent itself did his wrath rise, and then he lifted the discus that had come to him at Gomanta and hurled it. It struck the king of Karavira in the breast, pierced him through, and returned to Krishna's hand as a hawk returns to the wrist. Shrigala, who an hour before had been the emperor of the world, fell from his chariot like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt, and lay bleeding on the field.

His army broke. Some fled, some entered the city weeping, and some would not leave their fallen king and stood bewailing him where he lay. And Krishna, raising the hand that bore the discus, spoke to them all in a voice like the rumbling of clouds: "Do not fear! Do not fear."

It took a moment for the words to mean anything. Then the people of Karavira, looking from their slain king to the man who had slain him and yet told them not to fear, began to weep, the ministers and the citizens, and the queens who came out of the city with their sons, striking their breasts and crying over the king who would not rise again.

Among them came the queen Padmavati, and with her the boy prince Shakradeva, Shrigala's son. She did not come to curse. She came to the victor of the field and pleaded for her son.

And Krishna, looking at the boy who had lost everything in one afternoon, said: "This son of Shrigala is as my own. I declare safety to you all."

Then, in the sight of the weeping city, the victor did what no conqueror in that land was expected to do. He lifted the prince onto the throne of Karavira, the throne his father had been so sure of defending, and sprinkled him with celestial water, and anointed him king of the city that an hour before had been his enemy's.

The young king sat very straight on the great seat, his mother's hand on his shoulder, and the people of Karavira, who had come out prepared only to mourn, found themselves staring at a boy who was now their king and at the man who had given him the crown. Whatever they had feared from the fall of Shrigala, it was not this.
reflection: Shrigala had staked everything on the idea that one of the two men on that field must cease to exist: if Krishna fell, Shrigala would be the only Vasudeva, and if Shrigala fell, Krishna would be. Krishna answered the wager not by wiping out the loser's line but by adopting it, making the slain king's son his own and placing him on the throne, so that in the end neither Vasudeva was destroyed and the boy inherited his father's crown instead of his father's war.
next_story_tease: Far away at Kundina, the kings were gathering for the swayamvara, and Jarasandha had a warning for them all.
hero_scene: Krishna sprinkling celestial water over the young prince Shakradeva, seated on the great throne of Karavira, while the queen Padmavati watches with her hand on her son's shoulder and the grieving citizens of the city look on.
